title: Acceptance by black musicians and Leeman's racial outlook
summary: Leeman says he had no racial problems; black musicians took him under their wing, and Ellington and Basie were his idols.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: MR. LEEMAN: I don't want anybody to get the wrong idea of how I put this together. As I said before, I had no background with racial disturbance, and when I went to Kansas City and made all these beautiful friends and all these wonderful people who took me with open arms and under their wing, musically -- and I wondered why, I couldn't figure out whether or not I was a very fortunate person that they accepted me musically. So I had no racial problems with it.
I had a feeling in my heart, was all, as a lot of people do have, predominantly among the swing players there

When I was on the road, I used to buy records, my one love was Duke Ellington's band, that was before Basie came back into recording. And that was the epitome to me, and of course, Basie became my idol. Those were the two, really, because when he came back, he started recording.
And these people taking me under their wing -- that's why over the years I ended up playing with 2 and so forth, and I'm not getting ahead of myself.
But I had no qualms and I had no antagonistic racial feelings, which God was very good to me.
